approachQuestion.prompt:
Calibrate the Signed Samples

A nondecreasing integer array samples may contain negative values. Return a fresh nondecreasing array containing the square of each sample, preserving multiplicity. The inputs must remain unchanged.

Example 1: samples=[−5,−2,0,3] → [0,4,9,25].
Example 2: samples=[−4,−4] → [16,16].
Example 3: samples=[2,6] → [4,36].

Constraints:
1 ≤ n=samples.length ≤ 200,000; −1,000,000 ≤ samples[i] ≤ 1,000,000.
Use arithmetic that represents squared values through 10^12 exactly.
Output must be sorted and contain exactly n values.
constraints: Use arithmetic that represents squared values through 10^12 exactly.
Output must be sorted and contain exactly n values.

options.text: Allocate n output slots. Compare absolute values at the two remaining input ends, write the larger square into the last unfilled output slot, and move only the selected end inward. Continue until all slots are filled.
options.feedback: In a sorted interval the greatest absolute value occurs at an end. Filling output backward therefore places the greatest remaining square in its final position, including duplicates.

options.text: Create the output by squaring every sample, then comparison-sort that array into nondecreasing order.
options.feedback: This is correct but performs removable sorting work; the input’s order lets the two ends expose the greatest remaining square directly.

options.text: Square every sample and return those squares in original input order.
options.feedback: Squaring reverses magnitude order among negative values. [−5,−2] would produce [25,4], which is not sorted.

options.text: Compare the two remaining end squares, append the smaller one to output, and move that end inward.
options.feedback: The smallest square may be inside the interval. For [−5,0,3], this starts with 9 even though 0 must come first.

feedback.reason: Squaring does not preserve signed sort order: a large negative endpoint may produce the largest square.
details: Compare absolute values at the two ends of the unconsumed sorted interval. Write the greater square into the last vacant output position, then consume that end. Repeat until no values remain.

Squaring does not preserve signed sort order: a large negative endpoint may produce the largest square. The largest remaining magnitude is at an end, so place its square at the last free output slot. Filling forward with that maximum would reverse the required order.

“Allocate n output slots. Compare absolute values at the two remaining input ends, write the larger square into the last unfilled output slot, and move only the selected end inward. Continue until all slots are filled.”: In a sorted interval the greatest absolute value occurs at an end. Filling output backward therefore places the greatest remaining square in its final position, including duplicates.

“Create the output by squaring every sample, then comparison-sort that array into nondecreasing order.”: This is correct but performs removable sorting work; the input’s order lets the two ends expose the greatest remaining square directly.
“Square every sample and return those squares in original input order.”: Squaring reverses magnitude order among negative values. [−5,−2] would produce [25,4], which is not sorted.

“Compare the two remaining end squares, append the smaller one to output, and move that end inward.”: The smallest square may be inside the interval. For [−5,0,3], this starts with 9 even though 0 must come first.

complexityQuestion.prompt: For the fixed method “Fill Squared Output from the Back”, choose the tightest worst-case time and auxiliary-space pair. Let n be the input length. Fixed-width absolute value, multiplication through 10^12, indexed access and assignment cost constant time. Include allocation and all writes. Exclude input and the returned array; include the two end indices, output index and stack. No sorting, recursion, hashing or helper arrays are used.
constraints: Use arithmetic that represents squared values through 10^12 exactly.
Output must be sorted and contain exactly n values.

options.text: O(n log n) time, O(1) auxiliary space.

feedback.reason: Consume one endpoint and fill one result slot per iteration.
details: Each iteration consumes exactly one input value and fills one output slot, so there are n iterations. The result allocation has the same linear bound. The excluded output is the only growing array; the end and write indices are fixed helper state.
The option “O(n) time, O(1) auxiliary space.”: Every sample is consumed once while filling the result backward.
The option “O(n log n) time, O(1) auxiliary space.”: The fixed method exploits the input order and performs no sort.
The option “O(n) time, O(n) auxiliary space.”: This counts the returned array as auxiliary despite its explicit exclusion.
The option “O(n²) time, O(1) auxiliary space.”: No iteration scans the remaining interval.
